analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour over seven years and ends tipped and disability subminimum wages.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 231–199 in July 2019, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage in annual steps from $7.25 to $15 an hour over seven years, then keep it rising with median wage growth [S5]. It would also phase out the lower minimum wages now allowed for tipped workers, newly hired teenagers, and workers with disabilities, so everyone covered would eventually be paid the same federal floor [S4][S5]. The House passed it 231–199, but the Senate never took it up and it died when the Congress ended [S7][S9].
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum of $7.25 — including millions in food service, retail, and care work — would get scheduled raises reaching $15 an hour [S5]. Tipped workers now guaranteed as little as a $2.13 cash wage from employers would move to the full minimum [S5]. Teens under 20 and workers with disabilities, both currently payable below the minimum under federal certificates, would be phased up to the full wage, with technical assistance offered to employers of disabled workers to keep them employed [S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage, tipped, teen, and disabled workers

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in annual steps starting at $8.40 and reaching $15.00 six years later, with further increases after that tied to growth in the median hourly wage so the floor does not erode again as it did after 2009.

Phases out the tipped minimum wage, which lets employers pay tipped employees a cash wage as low as $2.13 as long as tips make up the difference; tipped workers would eventually be guaranteed the full federal minimum, and the bill affirms workers' right to keep their tips.
Ends the separate lower wage for newly hired workers under 20, currently set at $4.25, phasing them up to the standard minimum.

Ends the program allowing employers to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage: wages under Section 14(c) certificates would rise on a six-year schedule, no new certificates could be issued, the program would sunset, and the Labor Department would help employers transition these workers to regular jobs.

Requires the Labor Department to publish each increase 60 days before it takes effect, and requires a Government Accountability Office study of how the increases affect businesses, including small ones, with Congress directed to assess the findings and consider delaying later steps if warranted.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum or near-minimum wages — especially restaurants and food service, retail, and residential care — would bear higher payroll costs, with no exemption for very small businesses; a proposal to exempt firms with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales failed 210–218 [S7][S8]. Some cost would likely reach consumers through prices, and economists warned that some employers would respond by cutting jobs, hours, or automation. The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office, in an analysis widely reported at the time, projected the $15 floor would lift pay for roughly 27 million workers while costing about 1.3 million jobs. The bill itself required a GAO report on employment and business effects and directed Congress to consider delaying scheduled increases if the findings warranted it [S4][S5].

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes the same wage floor nationwide with no exemption or slower path for very small or low-margin businesses; an amendment to shield enterprises with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in annual sales failed on a near-party-line vote of 210–218, leaving even the smallest employers on the full seven-year schedule.

Employers — concentrated in restaurants, retail, and care work — absorb the full cost of the increases, and critics warned of job and hour losses in low-wage regions; the bill's own GAO-report provision, tracking effects on employment, turnover, prices, and small businesses, acknowledged those possible impacts and directed Congress to consider delaying later increases.

Ending the Section 14(c) subminimum raised a genuine concern that some employers of workers with disabilities might stop employing them rather than pay full minimum wages; the bill responds with transition assistance and a requirement to protect continuing employment opportunities, but the outcome for those workers depended on that assistance working.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and concrete: a wage floor stuck at $7.25 since 2009 would more than double for the lowest-paid workers, and three groups long excluded from full protection — tipped workers, teenagers, and workers with disabilities — would be brought inside it. The costs are real but narrower and harder to pin down: higher labor costs for low-wage employers, some price increases, and, per widely reported CBO analysis, roughly 1.3 million jobs foregone against roughly 27 million workers getting raises. The bill's gradual seven-year phase-in and built-in review process were reasonable design choices, but the absence of any small-business or regional adjustment is a fair criticism, and the disability subminimum repeal carries genuine transition risk. On balance, this is a bill whose gains for tens of millions of low-paid workers outweigh its costs, while honestly acknowledging that some of those costs fall on small employers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it, but the Senate majority never brought it up for a vote, and it simply expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Committee on Education and Labor approved the bill on a 28–20 vote in March 2019 and reported it in July, and the House debated and passed it on July 18, 2019, 231–199.

Before final passage, a Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add a small-business exemption failed 210–218, with 195 of 196 Republicans voting yes and 218 of 232 Democrats voting no.

The Senate received the bill the same day and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on July 22, 2019; no committee action, debate, or vote ever followed for the rest of the 116th Congress, and it died there when the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
The bill had 205 cosponsors, all Democrats, and passed the House with only 3 Republican votes; the Senate, where Republicans held the majority, took no action of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senate Republicans and the employers who would have faced the higher wage floor — particularly restaurants, retailers, and sheltered workshops paying subminimum wages — are better off, because the wage increase never took effect. The roughly 27 million workers who would have gotten raises are worse off.

for.name: Bobby Scott
for.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and Labor; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, guided it through his committee to a 28–20 favorable report, and managed floor consideration.

for.name: House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Provided nearly all the votes for passage, 228–6, including the rule that brought the bill to the floor.

for.name: Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Her majority brought the rule (H. Res. 492) to the floor and scheduled the bill for a vote, which passed 231–199.

for.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
for.what_they_did: Marked up the bill on March 6, 2019, and reported it amended by a 28–20 vote.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought H.R. 582 to the Senate floor for debate or a vote; after the House passed it, the bill sat on the Senate calendar under General Orders with no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill nearly unanimously, 192–3, and offered the failed motion to recommit seeking a small-business exemption.

against.name: Rep. Dan Meuser
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add an exemption for businesses with fewer than 10 employees and under $1 million in sales; the motion failed 210–218.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 228 of 234 Democrats voted yes while only 3 of 195 Republicans did, and the small-business motion to recommit passed only among Republicans, 195–14.

industries.note: The industry is the largest employer of minimum- and tipped-wage workers and relies on the $2.13 tipped cash wage; the bill phases that credit out and requires the full minimum by a set date, raising labor costs materially. Workers' gain and the industry's cost are the same dollars.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and other holders of disability subminimum certificates
industries.note: Employers holding Section 14(c) certificates could pay workers with disabilities below the minimum wage; the bill would raise their required wages on a fixed schedule, ban new certificates, and end the program outright, with transition assistance instead of the subminimum option.

industries.industry: Retail, residential care, and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These industries employ large numbers of workers near the $7.25 floor and would absorb the scheduled increases with no small-business exemption, passing some cost to prices or reducing hours and hiring.
